title: A Roll Call of Defeated Kings
overview: This chapter pauses the story to list every king Israel defeated, first east of the Jordan River under Moses and then west of it under Joshua.

parts.label: Lands east of the Jordan (v. 1)
parts.note: The list starts with the region east of the river, stretching from the Arnon gorge in the south to Mount Hermon in the north. These earlier victories, won before Joshua took over, are deliberately counted alongside his own.

parts.label: King Sihon's realm (vv. 2-3)
parts.note: Sihon was an Amorite king who ruled from the city of Heshbon over land east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. His defeat is told in Numbers 21, and this summary matches the earlier account.

parts.label: King Og's realm (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: Og ruled Bashan, the fertile high country to the north, with royal cities at Ashtaroth and Edrei. He is called one of the last of the Rephaites, an older people remembered elsewhere in the Bible as very tall, though little is known about them for certain.

parts.label: Moses hands out the east (v. 6)
parts.note: Moses gave this eastern land to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and to half of the tribe of Manasseh, who had asked to settle there (Numbers 32). Mentioning it here sets the pattern for what Joshua is about to do with the land west of the river.

parts.label: Joshua's territory (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: West of the Jordan, the conquered area runs from Baal Gad near Lebanon in the north to Mount Halak near Edom in the south, across hills, lowlands, valleys and desert. It names six peoples who lived there, while other passages list seven.

parts.label: Thirty-one kings (vv. 9-24)
parts.note: Each of these kings ruled a single city and its surrounding villages, and the list roughly follows the order of the campaigns: Jericho and Ai, then the southern alliance, then the northern one. Later chapters admit that some of these cities, such as Jerusalem and Gezer, stayed in Canaanite hands, and scholars debate how closely this tidy summary matches what actually happened on the ground.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this record of conquest should be read as straightforward history of wars God commanded, or as a stylized national account whose sweeping claims and violence need to be read more cautiously.
think: Why do you think people keep careful records of past victories, and what do such records do for the ones who keep them?
